summary: This note introduces the Texas–Indian wars, describing the Comanche as the most powerful Indian nation in the region, whose territory, the Comancheria, was persistently hostile to Spanish, Mexican, and Texan authorities. It states the article's scope: conflicts from 1820, just before Mexican independence from Spain, until 1875, when the last free band of Plains Indians, the Comanches led by Quahadi warrior Quanah Parker, surrendered and moved to the Fort Sill reservation in Oklahoma.
one_line: Overview of the Texas–Indian wars from 1820 to 1875, centered on Comanche resistance and the 1875 surrender of Quanah Parker's Quahadi band.
key_facts: Several Indian tribes occupied territory in the Texas area, but the preeminent nation was the Comanche.
The Comanche were known as the "Lords of the Plains."
The Comanche territory was called the Comancheria.
The Comancheria was described as the most powerful entity in the region.
The Comanche were persistently hostile to the Spanish, the Mexicans, and finally the Texans.
1820 is described as just before Mexico gained independence from Spain.
In 1875 the last free band of Plains Indians, the Comanches, surrendered.
The surrendering Comanche band was led by Quahadi warrior Quanah Parker.
After surrendering in 1875, the Comanches moved to the Fort Sill reservation in Oklahoma.
